reference.excerpt:
# serpapi-cli

> HTTP client for structured web search data via SerpApi

## Installation

### Homebrew (macOS/Linux)

```bash
brew tap serpapi/homebrew-tap
brew install serpapi-cli
```

### Pre-built Binaries

Download directly from [GitHub Releases](https://github.com/serpapi/serpapi-cli/releases)

### Go (compile from source)

```bash
go install github.com/serpapi/serpapi-cli/cmd/serpapi@latest
```

## Quick Start

```bash
# Authenticate
serpapi login

# Perform a search
serpapi search engine=google q=coffee
```

## Commands

### search

Perform a search with any supported SerpApi engine. Parameters are passed as bare `key=value` pairs.

```bash
# Basic search
serpapi search engine=google q=coffee

# Multiple parameters
serpapi search engine=google q="coffee shops" location="Austin,TX"

# Use a different engine
serpapi search engine=google_maps q="pizza" ll="@40.7455096,-74.0083012,14z"

# With server-side field filtering (reduces response size at API level)
serpapi search --fields "

# ASC CLI skills

A collection of Agent Skills for shipping with the [asc cli](https://github.com/rorkai/App-Store-Connect-CLI) (`asc`). These skills help agents run builds, TestFlight, metadata, submissions, signing, and Apple Ads workflows.

asc install-skills
```

```bash

claude plugin marketplace add rorkai/app-store-connect-cli-skills
claude plugin install asc@rorkai
```

# SimliClient

Simli WebRTC frontend client

### Installation

```bash
npm install simli-client
```

### Methods
- `Initialize(config: SimliClientConfig)`: Initializes the SimliClient with the provided configuration.
- `start()`: Sets up the WebRTC connection and prepares for streaming.
- `close()`: Closes the WebRTC connection and cleans up resources.
- `sendAudioData(audioData: Uint8Array)`: Sends audio data to the server.
- `listenToMediastreamTrack(stream: MediaStreamTrack)`: Listens to a MediaStreamTrack and sends audio data to the server. *Can be used as an alternative to `sendAudioData`.*
- `ClearBuffer()`: Clears the audio buffer, best used when you want the avatar to stop talking.

### Events
- `connected`
- `disconnected`
- `failed`

### Docs
[Setup guide](https://docs.simli.com/api-reference/simli-client)

# signal-cli

signal-cli is a commandline interface for the [Signal messenger](https://signal.org/).
It supports registering, verifying, sending and receiving messages.

# osx-wifi-cli

A command line tool for managing wifi connections on OSX

* * *
### Installation
```bash
$ npm install -g osx-wifi-cli
```
* * *
### Usage

`osx-wifi-cli` shows name of current connected network.

`osx-wifi-cli network` shows information about current connected network.

`osx-wifi-cli pass` shows password for current connected network.

`osx-wifi-cli scan` shows available networks.

`osx-wifi-cli on`, `osx-wifi-cli off`, and `osx-wifi-cli restart` control the wifi device state.

`osx-wifi-cli NETWORK PASSWORD` tries to connects to NETWORK with PASSWORD.

### Notes
* For easier use, add to your `.bashrc` file: `alias wifi='osx-wifi-cli'`

reference.excerpt:
# Clippy 📎

Copy files from your terminal that actually paste into GUI apps. No more switching to Finder.

**macOS only** - built specifically for the Mac clipboard system.

## Why Clippy?

`pbcopy` copies file _contents_, but GUI apps need file _references_. When you `pbcopy < image.png`, you can't paste it into Slack or email - those apps expect files, not raw bytes.

Clippy bridges this gap by detecting what you want and using the right clipboard format:

```bash
# Copy files as references (paste into any GUI app)
clippy report.pdf         # ⌘V into Slack/email - uploads the file
clippy *.jpg             # Multiple files at once

# Pipe data as files
curl -sL https://picsum.photos/300 | clippy  # Download → clipboard as file

# Copy your most recent download (immediate)
clippy -r                # Grabs the file you just downloaded
clippy -r 3              # Copy 3 most recent downloads

# Interactive picker for recent files
clippy -i               # Choose from list of recent downl

evidence: README describes npx deepagents-cli-codex-skill init and --personal/--path/--force flags.
Repo is TypeScript with src/cli.ts, templates/skills/deepagents-cli, MIT license, npm badge.
GitHub metadata: 1 star, 0 forks, 0 issues.
uncertainty: npm download volume and package security beyond Socket listing were not independently verified.
Whether skill markdown stays current with LangChain docs over time is unverified.
aiReview.tagline: Scaffold a Codex skill for LangChain Deep Agents CLI
aiReview.description: Installs structured Codex skill docs covering Deep Agents CLI commands, providers, sandboxes, and SDK customization.
pros: MIT-licensed TypeScript package with an npx init CLI for workspace or personal skill install.
cons: Very low GitHub traction (1 star, 0 forks, 0 issues) and limited independent adoption signal.
Does not implement Deep Agents itself; it copies documentation-derived skill files into .agents/skills.
Update path never overwrites existing files, so stale skill content may linger after upgrades.

aiReview.summary: Python hook pack that plays audio on Codex CLI lifecycle events (session, prompts, tools, compact). Small maintained GitHub repo with OS install notes and tests; useful as a companion, not a standalone CLI.
evidence: Repo description: codex cli hooks - adding voice on each hook; Python; 72 stars, 8 forks.
README lists SessionStart, UserPromptSubmit, PreToolUse, PermissionRequest, PostToolUse, Stop, PreCompact, PostCompact.
install/READMEs for mac/linux/windows and tests/test_hooks.py present.
Discovered repeatedly from RoggeOhta/awesome-codex-cli curated README.
uncertainty: Cannot verify sound quality, hook reliability across Codex versions, or license from the fetched README excerpt.
YouTube/LinkedIn badges in README are href="#" so those channels are unverified.
aiReview.tagline: Audio feedback for Codex CLI lifecycle hooks
aiReview.description: Install Python hooks that play sounds on session start, prompts, tool use, permissions, stop, and compact events.
pros: Documents eight Codex CLI hooks with matching sound files and a Python runner.
Provides Mac, Linux, and Windows install JSON plus a changelog tied to Codex CLI versions.
Includes a tests/test_hooks.py file and hook config under .codex/hooks.
Listed from a curated awesome-codex-cli README with 72 stars.
cons: Not a general-purpose CLI; it only customizes Codex CLI hook audio.
README leans on SVG/image instructions and placeholder social links.
Running third-party hooks inside an agent CLI still requires trusting local script execution.

aiReview.summary: MIT TypeScript MCP server that wraps OpenAI Codex CLI for Claude Code, with ask/exec/apply-diff tools and sandbox modes. Small (21 stars) wrapper; depends on Codex CLI plus ChatGPT or API auth.
evidence: GitHub README: MCP server for Claude Code + OpenAI Codex CLI; MIT; TypeScript.
Stars 21, forks 6, issues 4 as of fetch.
Listed in RoggeOhta/awesome-codex-cli curated README.
Install: npm @openai/codex then claude mcp add ... npx -y codex-cli-mcp-tool.
uncertainty: Last commit recency and npm publish status not verified beyond the repo page.
Whether tests exist despite README npm test mention was not confirmed by running them.
Actual Codex model names and ChatGPT $20/GPT-5 claims were not independently verified.
aiReview.tagline: MCP bridge from Claude Code to Codex CLI
aiReview.description: Expose Codex CLI to Claude Code via MCP with ask, exec, and apply-diff tools plus configurable sandbox modes.
pros: README documents installation via npx/claude mcp add, env vars, and Codex CLI as a required dependency.
Exposes ask-codex, exec-codex, apply-diff, and small utility tools with sandbox and approval options.
Repository is MIT-licensed TypeScript with a src/tools layout and CHANGELOG.
Notes ChatGPT login or OPENAI_API_KEY for authentication.
cons: Only 21 stars, 6 forks, and 4 issues; maintenance and production readiness are unclear.
danger-full-access sandbox can grant broad system access if misconfigured.
Requires both Codex CLI and Claude Code; it is a thin wrapper, not a standalone CLI.
README claims gpt-5 as default/only model, which may drift from actual Codex CLI support.

aiReview.summary: MIT-licensed MCP server that searches, ranks, and fetches agent-oriented docs for 420+ APIs via clirank.dev, with stdio npx and a hosted Fly.io endpoint. Small GitHub footprint (6 stars) so treat as a useful agent add-on, not a proven production staple.
evidence: GitHub: MIT, JavaScript/TypeScript, 6 stars, 0 forks, 1 issue.
README: npx -y clirank-mcp-server@latest; connects to https://clirank.dev/api; hosted https://clirank-mcp.fly.dev/mcp.
Listed in RoggeOhta/awesome-codex-cli curated README.
uncertainty: Cannot verify live API coverage, ranking quality, or hosted-endpoint uptime from the repo page alone.
Maintenance cadence beyond file presence is not independently verified.
aiReview.tagline: MCP tools to search, rank, and document APIs for agents
aiReview.description: Expose search, recommend, compare, docs, and review tools over 420+ APIs so coding agents pick integrations from live CLIRank data.
pros: README documents MCP tools (discover, recommend, docs, compare, reviews) and install paths for Claude Code, Codex CLI, Cursor, and other stdio clients.
MIT-licensed TypeScript/JavaScript repo with npx entrypoint and a hosted MCP URL.
No CLIRank API key is required for the documented client path.
cons: Only 6 stars and 0 forks; community traction is limited.
Depends on the remote clirank.dev API, so results and availability are not self-contained.

aiReview.summary: Emacs Lisp package that runs Codex CLI in project-scoped terminals with send helpers and a multi-session layout. MIT-licensed, documented, and tested; niche to Emacs users who already have Codex on PATH.
evidence: GitHub README: Run Codex CLI inside Emacs with project-scoped terminals and send helpers.
Language Emacs Lisp; files include tests/codex-cli-test.el and .github/workflows/ci.yml.
Stars 30, forks 3, issues 2, license MIT.
Discovered from RoggeOhta/awesome-codex-cli curated README.
uncertainty: Whether the package is actually published on MELPA.
Maintenance cadence and issue resolution quality beyond listed file inventory.
Runtime behavior of send/chunking against current Codex CLI versions.
aiReview.tagline: Project-scoped Codex terminals inside Emacs
aiReview.description: Run Codex CLI in Emacs with project sessions, side windows, and commands to send prompts, regions, or files.
pros: README documents install, commands, window/session behavior, send styles, and troubleshooting.
Repository includes ERT tests, CI workflow, Eask, and an MIT license.
Supports vterm with a built-in term fallback and configurable send chunking.
cons: Only 30 stars and 3 forks, so community adoption is still small.
Requires Emacs 28+ and a Codex CLI binary on PATH, so it is not a standalone CLI.
MELPA availability is mentioned as optional and not independently verified here.

aiReview.summary: JetBrains plugin (Kotlin + VS Code extension host) that runs VS Code coding agents such as Roo Code, Cline, and Kilo Code inside IntelliJ-family IDEs. Listed under awesome-codex-cli but it is an IDE plugin, not a command-line tool.
evidence: GitHub: haleclipse/codex-jetbrains, Kotlin, Apache-2.0, ~124 stars.
README describes JetBrains plugin + extension_host, marketplace install, and VS Code agent compatibility.
Discovered from RoggeOhta/awesome-codex-cli as Haleclipse/Codex-JetBrains.
uncertainty: Whether haleclipse/codex-jetbrains is a fork, rename, or mirror of wecode-ai/RunVSAgent.
Current maintenance, Marketplace listing freshness, and Codex-CLI-specific integration quality.
aiReview.tagline: Run VS Code coding agents inside JetBrains IDEs
aiReview.description: Host VS Code-based coding agents in IntelliJ-family IDEs via a Kotlin plugin and Node.js extension host with RPC.
pros: Apache 2.0 Kotlin plugin plus Node.js extension host with documented RPC architecture.
Installable from JetBrains Marketplace (plugin 28068) and GitHub releases.
Documents support for multiple JetBrains IDEs from 2023.1 and agents including Roo Code, Cline, and Kilo Code.
cons: Not a CLI; poor fit for a command-line/awesome-codex-cli style list.
README branding (RunVSAgent / other GitHub org) does not match the haleclipse/codex-jetbrains canonical URL.
Modest community signal (about 124 stars, 4 forks, 1 issue) and known-issues docs imply compatibility gaps.

aiReview.summary: GitHub-backed tmux session manager for Codex, Claude, Gemini, and custom agent CLIs, with save/restore, logging, and optional loopers. Fits a CLI/productivity directory; modest stars and setup complexity warrant a human look, not rejection.
evidence: GitHub description: tmux manager for running, monitoring, saving, restoring, and looping Codex, Claude, Gemini, and custom agent CLIs.
README documents features, requirements (Bash 3.2+, Python 3.10+, tmux), and setup.sh behavior.
Repo shows MIT license, tests/, docs/, bin/, pyproject.toml, 34 stars, 173 commits.
Discovered repeatedly from RoggeOhta/awesome-codex-cli curated README.
uncertainty: Live CI status and recent commit recency beyond the HTML snapshot.
Runtime quality of save/restore and loopers without executing the tool.
Whether hook merges into Codex/Claude/Gemini configs are always safe for all users.
aiReview.tagline: Tmux farm for coding-agent CLIs with save/restore
aiReview.description: Manage, monitor, snapshot, and loop Codex, Claude, Gemini, and custom agent CLIs in persistent tmux sessions with logging.
pros: Public GitHub repo with MIT license, README, tests, CONTRIBUTING, and 173 commits.
Documents tmux session management, monitoring, snapshot/restore, and prompt loopers for multiple agent CLIs.
Includes setup.sh, docs, examples, integrations, and GitHub workflows.
Listed from a curated awesome-codex-cli README rather than a generic blog post.
cons: Only 34 stars and 1 fork, so community adoption is still small.
Setup writes helper scripts, PATH, and provider hook files, which is more invasive than a simple CLI install.
Requires tmux plus provider binaries; several features are optional extras (systemd, multitail, deep-history).

aiReview.summary: Community Vercel AI SDK provider that talks to OpenAI Codex CLI (exec or app-server) using ChatGPT Plus/Pro OAuth or an API key. Solid GitHub/npm library with documented limits, Node-only spawning, and tight Codex CLI version pins.
evidence: GitHub description: community provider for Codex CLI via spawn; MIT license; 40 commits; npm package ai-sdk-provider-codex-cli.
README documents two providers, AI SDK v7 LanguageModelV4, listModels, and authentication via codex login.
Discovered repeatedly from RoggeOhta/awesome-codex-cli curated README.
uncertainty: Exact last-commit calendar date and npm download volume not independently verified.
Runtime security of sandbox/approval defaults versus Codex CLI ToS for subscription reuse not audited.
aiReview.tagline: Vercel AI SDK provider wrapping local Codex CLI
aiReview.description: Connect Vercel AI SDK generate/stream APIs to Codex CLI via spawn or JSON-RPC, using ChatGPT OAuth or OPENAI_API_KEY.
pros: MIT-licensed TypeScript package with README, CHANGELOG, LIMITATIONS, examples, tests, and npm distribution.
Supports generateText, streamText, and generateObject via codexExec and persistent app-server modes.
Documents Node >= 22, ESM-only, Codex CLI 0.156.x pinning, and AI SDK v4–v7 version tags.
Listed in awesome-codex-cli and shows ongoing commits plus ~70 stars and 11 forks.
cons: It is a Node library that spawns Codex CLI, not a standalone command-line app.
Requires a ChatGPT Plus/Pro login or API key and a matching local Codex CLI version.
Node-only process spawn is unsuitable for browsers and depends on ~/.codex/auth.json.

aiReview.summary: Go proxy that exposes CLI/OAuth provider sessions as OpenAI/Gemini/Claude-compatible HTTP APIs. Popular and actively maintained, but the free-CLI-to-API pattern raises provider ToS and account-sharing risk.
evidence: GitHub description and README: wrap Antigravity, Codex, Claude Code, Grok Build, Muse, Devin as compatible APIs.
~55k stars, ~8.4k forks, MIT license, 4000+ commits, Go module layout with cmd/, Dockerfile, and docs.
Discovered from awesome-codex-cli and awesome-gemini-cli curated READMEs.
uncertainty: Whether current releases still work against each vendor CLI after ToS or auth changes.
Exact legal status of using CLI OAuth quotas as an API gateway.
Operational security of Management API defaults was not audited.
aiReview.tagline: Local OpenAI-compatible proxy over CLI OAuth accounts
aiReview.description: Run a local proxy that maps CLI and OAuth AI accounts to OpenAI, Gemini, Claude, and Codex-compatible APIs with multi-account routing.
pros: MIT-licensed Go project with Docker, config examples, docs, and a large public GitHub footprint.
Exposes OpenAI/Gemini/Claude/Codex-style endpoints with streaming, tools, multimodal input, and multi-account load balancing.
Appears in multiple curated CLI awesome lists and ships a reusable Go SDK plus management docs.
cons: README markets wrapping consumer CLI/OAuth sessions as free API access, which likely conflicts with provider terms.
Heavy affiliate/relay-sponsor content in the README can obscure core usage.
Requires storing OAuth/CLI credentials locally, increasing account-compromise impact.

aiReview.summary: GitHub-backed Docker image that runs Claude, Codex, or Pi CLIs with an iptables allowlist. Useful as a sandboxing helper, not a general-purpose CLI; small star count and NET_ADMIN plus optional docker.sock mounts need care.
evidence: Repo description and README: claude, codex, pi CLI sandbox docker container.
106 commits on main; topics include claude-code, codex-cli, docker, llm-sandbox.
Usage requires --cap-add=NET_ADMIN --cap-add=NET_RAW and workspace bind-mounts.
uncertainty: License file not confirmed from the page extract.
Exact allowlist completeness and ongoing maintenance of IP lists not independently verified.
Default branch image freshness versus tagged releases not checked.
aiReview.tagline: Docker sandbox for LLM coding CLIs with outbound firewall
aiReview.description: Run Claude, Codex, or Pi CLIs in Docker with iptables blocking most outbound traffic except selected vendor and GitHub IPs.
pros: README documents docker run usage, volume mounts, and a shell alias wrapper.
Firewall intent is explicit: iptables allowlist for GitHub, Anthropic, and Google Cloud IPs.
Image is published at ghcr.io/libops/cli-sandbox with Dockerfile and CI-related files in-repo.
Optional Docker-in-sandbox path documents host-socket risk and --group-add GID handling.
cons: Only 5 stars and 1 fork, so community adoption is limited.
Requires NET_ADMIN and NET_RAW capabilities, which expands the container’s privilege surface.
Mounting the host Docker socket grants effectively root on the host if used.

aiReview.summary: Dockerized sandbox that runs Claude Code, Copilot, Codex, and gh behind an egress allowlist, MITM intercept, and ttyd web terminal, aimed at logging agent API traffic for research.
evidence: README describes docker compose, ./clide web/shell/claude, iptables allowlist, and intercept.jsonl schema.
GitHub metadata: Shell, MIT, 2 stars, files include Dockerfile, firewall.sh, SECURITY.md, RUNBOOK.md.
Listed in RoggeOhta/awesome-codex-cli curated README.
uncertainty: Cannot verify intercept completeness, token redaction, or firewall reliability without running the image.
Maintenance trajectory unclear given star count and unknown last-commit recency from this snapshot.
aiReview.tagline: Sandboxed multi-agent CLI with egress logs and MITM
aiReview.description: Run coding-agent CLIs in a Docker sandbox with an egress allowlist, intercept logs, and a browser terminal for session observability.
pros: MIT-licensed GitHub repo with Dockerfile, compose, wrapper script, and documented firewall/allowlist.
Bundles Claude Code, Copilot CLI, Codex CLI, gh, and glab with a ttyd web terminal and tmux.
Documents intercept, egress, and session-event JSONL streams plus a SECURITY.md threat model.
cons: Very low adoption (2 stars, 0 forks) and a single GitHub issue.
Requires NET_ADMIN, project bind-mount, and API tokens in .env; MITM captures full request/response bodies.
Research-oriented logging of agent traffic may be more than typical local CLI users want.

aiReview.summary: Small MIT-licensed bash CLI that zips and swaps ~/.codex profiles so Codex CLI users can switch named accounts. Useful niche helper with modest stars and only 11 commits; author notes primary testing on Mac.
evidence: GitHub description and README: switch/save/restore multiple OpenAI Codex CLI accounts.
Listed in RoggeOhta/awesome-codex-cli; MIT license; single script codex-accounts.sh.
Data locations documented: ~/.codex, ~/codex-data/<name>.zip, ~/.codex-switch/state and shared.
uncertainty: Cannot verify Linux/WSL behavior or ongoing maintenance beyond the public README and commit count.
Cannot audit the shell script for safe handling of auth tokens without a full code review.
aiReview.tagline: Zip-and-swap multiple Codex CLI login profiles
aiReview.description: Bash script that saves, lists, and switches named Codex CLI account folders via zip backups of ~/.codex.
pros: Provides list/current/save/add/switch commands around Codex CLI’s single-login ~/.codex layout.
MIT-licensed public GitHub repo with a documented install path and zip/unzip/bash requirements.
Keeps shared paths (rules, AGENTS.md, config.toml, skills, memories, automations) overlayed after switches.
cons: Repository is small (about 84 stars, 12 forks, 11 commits) and not a packaged distribution.
README states the author has tested it on Mac only, while also claiming Linux/WSL support.
Works by copying session data in ~/codex-data and ~/.codex, which is a local credential-handling workflow.

aiReview.summary: Python CLI that bulk-probes Codex auth files via a CLI Proxy management API, reports 401s and weekly quota, and can delete failed credentials after confirmation. Niche, small, and security-sensitive because it forwards real tokens to a probe URL.
evidence: GitHub description and README: batch Codex auth inspection via CLI Proxy Management API; stats for total/401/weekly quota; optional delete of 401 auth files.
Safety section: default https and host=chatgpt.com; --allow-unsafe-probe-host and --insecure/--allow-insecure-tls documented as high risk.
Listed in RoggeOhta/awesome-codex-cli curated README; 27 stars, 6 forks, 5 commits.
uncertainty: License file not confirmed from the listing page.
Maintenance cadence and production safety of cliproxy_scanner.py not audited.
Whether --delete-401 is strictly scoped to the operator’s own proxy instance.
aiReview.tagline: Bulk-scan Codex auths via CLI Proxy management API
aiReview.description: Probe CLI Proxy auth files, count 401s and weekly quota, optionally delete failed credentials after confirmation.
pros: Documents scan-only and delete-401 flows with required base URL and management key.
Includes probe-host HTTPS/chatgpt.com defaults and extra flags for unsafe hosts and insecure TLS.
Outputs JSON summary fields for totals, 401s, quota-zero, and status buckets.
cons: Very small repo (few commits, ~27 stars) with a single Python script and no apparent test suite.
Forwards real tokens through management api-call to a probe URL, which is high-risk if misconfigured.
README is Chinese-only and usage is tightly coupled to a specific CLI Proxy management API.

aiReview.summary: Vendor blog post about OpenAI Codex CLI with install notes and Apidog CTAs; not the CLI itself. Prefer the official GitHub/npm project over this marketing article.
evidence: Page title and body are a how-to for OpenAI Codex CLI hosted on apidog.com/blog.
Install command shown is npm install -g @openai/codex with link to github.com/openai/codex.
Rubric prefers GitHub-backed CLIs over generic blog posts; candidate type is web_url from a curated README.
Article links to apidog.com/blog/bypass-codex-sandbox/.
uncertainty: Accuracy of CLI flags and Node 22+ requirements versus current official docs was not independently verified.
Whether the awesome list intended the official Codex repo instead of this blog is unknown.
aiReview.tagline: Blog walkthrough of a terminal AI coding agent
aiReview.description: Explains OpenAI Codex CLI setup, approval modes, and use cases, with product promotion mixed in.
pros: Covers npm install, API key setup, approval modes, and example prompts for Codex CLI.
Points to the openai/codex GitHub repository as the source project.
Describes sandbox and approval-mode security options at a high level.
cons: The URL is an Apidog marketing article, not a maintained CLI or official docs.
Includes product CTAs and a linked guide on bypassing the Codex sandbox.
Content can go stale versus the official Codex repository.

evidence: Canonical URL is anothercodingblog.com Substack post dated Oct 05, 2025 by Taylor Ortiz.
Meta description matches a full Codex CLI guide: commands, AGENTS.md, workflows, MCP, CI/CD.
Listed from RoggeOhta/awesome-codex-cli README as Commands, Agents, and Advanced Workflows.
Rubric prefers maintained GitHub CLIs over generic blog guides.
uncertainty: Could not verify long-term maintenance or accuracy against current Codex CLI.
Paywalled remainder of the post (content truncated in fetch) may add or omit details.
Author expertise and independent review of the article are unknown.
aiReview.tagline: Guide to Codex CLI commands, agents, and workflows

pros: Covers slash commands such as /model, /approvals, /review, /init, /compact, /diff, and /mention.
Explains AGENTS.md as agent-oriented repo instructions with a Python example.
Describes approval/sandbox modes, MCP inspector usage, config.toml, and headless CI artifact workflows.
cons: It is a Substack blog post, not a GitHub-backed CLI or official docs.
Content can go stale as Codex CLI changes and includes a subscribe/paywall CTA.
Some claims (for example multi-hour runs) depend on OpenAI product posts rather than independently verified behavior.

aiReview.summary: Vendor tutorial covering OpenAI Codex CLI install, modes, and deployment-oriented workflows; useful as reading, not a maintained CLI to list as a tool.
evidence: URL is deployhq.com/blog getting-started article, Part 2 of a product series.
Content documents `@openai/codex`, approval modes, `/review`, MCP, and `codex exec`.
Listed from awesome-codex-cli README as “Deployment Workflows with Codex CLI (DeployHQ).”
uncertainty: Cannot verify accuracy of GPT-5.3-Codex claims against current OpenAI docs.
No independent maintenance or last-updated date beyond the live page.
aiReview.tagline: Tutorial on terminal Codex CLI for local agentic coding
aiReview.description: Explains installing and using OpenAI’s terminal coding agent for edits, tests, review, and CI-style headless runs.
pros: Covers install (npm, WSL), auth, approval modes, models, MCP, and headless `codex exec`.
Includes concrete prompt examples for refactor, tests, review, and Git piping.
States local-first file handling and ChatGPT-plan versus API-key auth.
cons: It is a DeployHQ marketing blog, not a GitHub-backed CLI or official docs.
Model names and feature claims may drift from upstream Codex CLI.
Rubric prefers the actual maintained CLI over generic getting-started posts.

aiReview.summary: GitHub awesome-list of OpenAI Codex CLI skills, subagents, plugins, and related docs; useful as a directory, not a CLI itself. Candidate title “Submit it!” is a self-link artifact.
evidence: https://github.com/RoggeOhta/awesome-codex-cli describes 150+/271 Codex CLI ecosystem resources.
About 547 stars, 328 forks, CC0-1.0, topics include awesome-list, cli, openai-codex.
README lists official OpenAI Codex docs plus community collections.
uncertainty: Whether listed third-party tools remain maintained or safe.
Last-commit freshness beyond the GitHub last-commit badge.
Whether this belongs in a CLI-focused directory versus a docs/resources section.
aiReview.tagline: Curated Codex CLI skills, agents, plugins, and docs
aiReview.description: Collects official docs, skills, subagents, plugins, MCP, and tutorials for OpenAI’s terminal coding agent.
pros: Public GitHub list with README sections covering official docs, skills, subagents, plugins, MCP, and tutorials.
CC0-1.0 license, CONTRIBUTING.md, and hundreds of stars and forks.
Claims hundreds of catalogued links organized by category rather than a single blog roundup.
cons: It is a curated markdown list, not a command-line tool.
Only 16 commits; link quality and maintenance of every listed item are not independently verified.
Discovery metadata used the self-referential “Submit it!” title instead of the repo name.

aiReview.summary: Vendor blog comparing Codex CLI and Gemini CLI, with a third-party pitch for UI Bakery. Useful as a short overview, but it is not a CLI and mixes marketing with some inaccurate product attribution.
evidence: canonicalUrl is a UI Bakery blog post titled Codex vs Gemini CLI.
Page markets UI Bakery as a bonus tool and includes signup/book-a-call CTAs.
Discovered from awesome-codex-cli README as a comparison link, not a tool listing.
Rubric prefers maintained GitHub CLIs over generic comparison blog posts.
uncertainty: Cannot verify technical claims about model providers, interruptibility, or enterprise tiers without running the CLIs.
Author expertise and update cadence beyond the November 20, 2025 date are unverified.
aiReview.tagline: Short blog comparison of two AI coding CLIs
aiReview.description: Compares Codex CLI and Gemini CLI features, use cases, and trade-offs, plus a vendor internal-tool alternative.
pros: Gives a concise side-by-side of Codex CLI versus Gemini CLI features and intended users.
Links to the OpenAI Codex GitHub repo and Gemini CLI site.
Includes a simple criteria table covering direction, learning curve, and integrations.
cons: It is a UI Bakery marketing article, not a maintained GitHub-backed CLI.
Misattributes Codex CLI as GitHub’s tool and ends in a product CTA.
Short (about 5 minutes) with limited depth versus primary docs.

aiReview.summary: Oh My Zsh plugins that add tab completion and aliases for Claude Code, Codex, and Gemini CLIs. Small MIT Shell repo (19 stars); useful for zsh users of those tools, but install docs still show a placeholder clone URL.
evidence: GitHub description and README: collection of intelligent Zsh completion plugins for Claude Code, Codex, and Gemini CLI.
Repo stats from GitHub API: 19 stars, 6 forks, 1 issue, language Shell, MIT License.
File tree includes claude/codex/gemini plugin.zsh files plus install.sh and uninstall.sh.
uncertainty: Whether completions stay in sync with current Claude/Codex/Gemini CLI flags.
Quality of install.sh .zshrc mutation beyond README claims.
Activity/maintenance cadence beyond snapshot metadata.
aiReview.tagline: Zsh completions and aliases for major AI CLIs
aiReview.description: Adds Oh My Zsh tab completion, aliases, and install/uninstall scripts for Claude Code, Codex, and Gemini CLI.
pros: MIT-licensed Shell plugins covering Claude Code, Codex, and Gemini CLI commands and aliases.
Includes install.sh, uninstall.sh, and notes on backing up .zshrc.
README documents Tab completions, MCP-related commands, and troubleshooting for zcompdump.
cons: Only 19 stars and 6 forks; maintenance and completeness of completions versus upstream CLIs are unclear.
Quick-install clone URL in the README still uses YOUR_USERNAME/ohmyzsh-plugins.
Requires Oh My Zsh plus at least one of the three vendor CLIs.

aiReview.summary: Maintained MIT Nix flake that packages OpenAI Codex CLI as native Rust binaries (plus optional Node) with hourly updates, Cachix, and flake/NixOS/Home Manager install paths.
evidence: Repo description: Nix flake for OpenAI Codex CLI, native Rust binary, hourly updates, multi-platform caching; 163 stars, MIT, Shell.
README documents nix run github:sadjow/codex-cli-nix, flake integration, and platforms x86_64/aarch64 linux/darwin.
Files include flake.nix, package.nix, update workflows, and tests/.
uncertainty: Live health of Cachix cache and latest packaged Codex version were not verified beyond README.
Security of auto-merge without required PR checks was not independently audited.
aiReview.tagline: Hourly-updated Nix flake for Codex CLI binaries
aiReview.description: Install OpenAI Codex CLI on Nix via native Rust binaries or bundled Node, with hourly updates and multi-platform Cachix caches.
pros: GitHub repo with MIT license, flake.nix, tests, and GitHub Actions for hourly version checks.
Documents nix run/profile, flake inputs, NixOS, Home Manager, and Cachix usage.
Default package is a native Rust binary for linux/darwin x86_64 and aarch64; optional Node package exists.
README explains auto-update flow, version tags, and caveats about following main before cache builds finish.
cons: It is a packaging/distribution wrapper, not a standalone CLI product.
README notes auto-merge on main without required PR checks and that following main can lag cache builds.
Cachix public-key placeholder in sample Nix config must be filled by the user.

aiReview.summary: MIT-licensed Go CLI that bridges a local clipboard over a loopback SSH reverse tunnel so remote Claude Code, Codex CLI, and similar agents can paste images and copy text. macOS-to-Linux is documented as stable; Windows is experimental and some agent paths are not fully smoke-tested.
evidence: GitHub: ShunmeiCho/cc-clip, ~173 stars, MIT, Go, CI and release workflows present.
README describes loopback-only RemoteForward, setup/doctor/serve commands, and agent target flags.
Discovered repeatedly from RoggeOhta/awesome-codex-cli curated README.
uncertainty: Cannot independently verify current release health, issue backlog quality, or real-world security of the reverse-tunnel path.
Exact latest version and download counts not fully confirmed beyond README badges.
aiReview.tagline: SSH clipboard bridge for remote AI coding agents
aiReview.description: Paste local clipboard images into remote Claude Code, Codex, and similar SSH sessions, and copy unwrapped text back.
pros: Go CLI with MIT license, tests, CI workflows, GoReleaser, and multi-language docs.
Documents setup for Claude Code, Codex, opencode, Cursor, and related notification integrations.
Stable path is specified as macOS 13+ to Linux with named SSH Host entries.
Listed from a curated awesome-codex-cli README rather than a generic blog post.
cons: Windows-to-Linux support is labeled experimental.
opencode/Antigravity host delivery and several agent paste paths are not end-to-end smoke-tested.
Codex setup may require remote sudo to install Xvfb.

aiReview.summary: Single Bash script that packs and unpacks Codex CLI home-directory auth data so you can sign in on a machine with a browser and copy credentials to a headless Linux host. Useful niche helper, but it is a one-file workflow with no applied license and inherent credential-handling risk.
evidence: GitHub: 49 stars, 1 fork, Shell, files README.md and codex-auth-transfer.sh.
README describes export/import CLI, rsync/cp fallback, and credential-bundle warnings.
Listed in RoggeOhta/awesome-codex-cli curated README.
uncertainty: Cannot verify script correctness or Codex still using those paths.
License is suggested (PolyForm NC) but not present in the repo.
Unknown maintenance beyond README claims.
aiReview.tagline: Transfer Codex CLI login data to headless Linux hosts
aiReview.description: Export Codex CLI config and auth dirs to a tarball and import them on a remote Linux server when browser login is unavailable.
pros: Documents export/import of ~/.config/codex, ~/.local/share/codex, and ~/.codex into a 600-permission tarball.
Import can backup existing dirs with --force and sets 700/600 permissions.
README covers Linux Mint export and AlmaLinux import plus secure-transport warnings.
cons: Repository is only the script and README; no tests, CI, or LICENSE file despite a non-commercial license suggestion.
Tokens may be machine-bound; the author notes transfers can fail.
Linux/Bash-only; 49 stars and one issue indicate a small, informal project.

aiReview.summary: MIT-licensed Codex CLI and Claude Code plugin that records verification receipts and reuses unchanged checks instead of rerunning full suites. Real, documented agent-workflow tooling with modest stars and a promotional badge on the README.
evidence: GitHub grapefruit0205/click: Python, MIT, 38 stars, CI badge, plugin marketplaces for Codex and Claude.
README describes Evidence mode, click-gate status/dashboard, and host hook install commands.
Source listing includes .codex-plugin, .claude-plugin, and extensive hook implementations.
uncertainty: Ongoing maintenance quality and security of host hooks beyond listed workflows.
Whether the repo is the canonical click.org/pallets Click CLI (it is not).
aiReview.tagline: Reuse verified checks across agent edit-test loops
aiReview.description: Records verification receipts and re-runs only checks whose evidence no longer holds, for Codex CLI and Claude Code.
pros: Ships as a Codex CLI and Claude Code plugin with a click-gate CLI, CI, MIT license, and v1.3.0 release notes.
Documents incremental verification, sharding, and language-specific support (pytest/unittest, Jest/Vitest, go test).
Includes status, dashboard, and reason codes so reuse vs rerun is inspectable.
cons: Small GitHub traction (38 stars, 2 forks) relative to a large plugin surface.
README includes an affiliate/promo badge that is unrelated to the core product.
Savings claims rest on a small fixture A/B, not production measurements.

aiReview.summary: GitHub Codex plugin that wraps the Tree Ring Memory CLI with a skill and lifecycle hooks for local-first agent memory. Niche, 0 stars, and not a standalone CLI, so it is a weak fit for a CLI-first list.
evidence: GitHub description: Codex plugin wrapper for Tree Ring Memory local-first agent memory lifecycle guidance.
README: plugin 0.3.10 requires tree-ring CLI >= 0.15.0; hooks need CLI 0.15.6+.
Repo shows 0 stars, 0 forks, 14 commits, MIT license.
uncertainty: Whether the OpenAI plugin directory listing is accepted.
Runtime quality of hooks and CLI integration beyond README claims.
Ongoing maintenance beyond recent commits.
aiReview.tagline: Codex skill and hooks for local-first agent memory
aiReview.description: Packages a Codex skill and lifecycle hooks that guide recall, write, audit, and forget using a local Tree Ring Memory CLI.
pros: MIT-licensed public repo with README, PRIVACY, TERMS, and SECURITY docs.
Documents version pins, SHA-256 installer verification, and no-pipe-to-shell install.
States it ships instructions and hooks only, with no MCP server, analytics, or transcript capture.
cons: Zero stars and forks; community adoption is unproven.
Depends on a separate Tree Ring Memory CLI and Codex/ChatGPT Work host trust.
Plugin wrapper rather than a standalone command-line app.

aiReview.summary: Maintained Go CLI (bkt) for Bitbucket Cloud and Data Center with gh-like commands, structured output, and packaging via Homebrew, WinGet, Scoop, Nix, and Go. Fits a CLI/tools directory; modest stars but real releases and CI.
evidence: GitHub description: Bitbucket CLI with gh-like ergonomics; topics include cli, bitbucket, golang.
README: brew install bitbucket-cli; binary bkt; Cloud and Data Center; MIT license.
237 stars, 49 forks, 537 commits, CI/release/Homebrew badges on README.
uncertainty: Current release cadence and issue backlog were not fully audited.
Runtime correctness against live Bitbucket APIs was not tested.
OpenSSF Scorecard numeric score was not fetched beyond the badge.
aiReview.tagline: gh-style CLI for Bitbucket Cloud and Data Center
aiReview.description: Run Bitbucket Cloud and Data Center workflows from the terminal with JSON/YAML output, auth, and packaging for common installers.
pros: Open-source MIT Go project with CI, codecov, goreleaser, and OpenSSF Scorecard badges.
Supports Bitbucket Cloud and Data Center and documents installers including Homebrew core, WinGet, Scoop, Nix, and go install.
README states a JSON/YAML contract aimed at scripts and coding agents.
Repository includes changelog, contributing, security policy, and 500+ commits.
cons: Community size is modest (~237 stars, 49 forks) relative to GitHub’s gh.
Homebrew core builds omit the OAuth client, so Cloud browser login needs extra env vars or the author’s tap.
Binary name bkt collides with an unrelated Rust caching tool of the same name.

aiReview.summary: MIT-licensed Go CLI (`jk`) for Jenkins REST operations: contexts, jobs, runs, logs, artifacts, and admin tasks. Early 0.x release with CI and docs; not the official jenkins-cli.jar.
evidence: github.com/avivsinai/jenkins-cli: Go, MIT, 92 stars, 11 forks.
README describes jk features, install paths, and status as of v0.0.36 (11 Aug 2026).
Repo includes cmd/jk, docs/spec.md, CI, goreleaser, and SECURITY.md.
uncertainty: Long-term maintenance and production battle-testing beyond README claims.
Exact OpenSSF Scorecard numeric score not verified in this pass.
aiReview.tagline: GitHub CLI–style Jenkins control from the terminal
aiReview.description: Operate Jenkins from the terminal: auth contexts, search jobs, trigger runs, stream logs, and manage nodes, queues, and plugins.
pros: Go binary with Homebrew, Scoop, go install, and GitHub release artifacts.
README documents auth, SSO/API tokens, job/run/log/artifact commands, and JSON/YAML output.
MIT license, CI, gitleaks, Scorecard, and changelog present on GitHub.
Explicitly distinguished from the official Jenkins JAR CLI.
cons: Still 0.x (v0.0.36); companion plugin, JCasC, events, and metrics are not in the binary.
Modest popularity (~92 stars) relative to core Jenkins tooling.
Requires Jenkins API tokens rather than browser SSO for scripted access.

aiReview.summary: Vendor Codex plugin that wraps the WaveSpeed MCP server and CLI so an agent can search models, quote prices, and generate image/video/audio/3D. Useful for Codex users on that platform; it is not a standalone CLI and generation is billed through WaveSpeed.
evidence: GitHub description and README: Codex plugin for WaveSpeed CLI media generation.

pros: Official documentation lists native SDKs, frameworks, model providers, and an OpenTelemetry endpoint.
Points to Python and JS/TS SDKs plus academy tracing material.
Site is maintained product documentation, not an abandoned gist or generic roundup.
cons: The page is a docs index, not a command-line app or self-hosted client.
Anchor title “Clients” from awesome-selfhosted does not describe this resource.
Does not itself ship a CLI; a Langfuse CLI is only mentioned in agent footer text.

aiReview.summary: Curated GitHub list of Halo CMS themes, plugins, and related ecosystem links—not a CLI or terminal utility. Poor fit for a command-line tools directory.
evidence: GitHub description: 与 Halo 相关的周边生态资源列表; topics awesome, awesome-list, halo.
About 628 stars, 121 forks, 221 commits on main.
README sections cover Halo 2.0 official/community themes and official/community plugins.
uncertainty: Last-commit recency and health of every linked community project were not fully audited.
License file presence was not confirmed from the listing page.
aiReview.tagline: Curated Halo CMS themes, plugins, and ecosystem links
aiReview.description: Collects official and community themes, plugins, and related resources for the Halo blogging CMS.
pros: Official halo-sigs repository listing Halo 2.0 themes and plugins with GitHub links.
Includes official starters plus a large community theme and plugin catalog.
Public repo with hundreds of stars, forks, and an ongoing commit history.
cons: It is an awesome-list, not a command-line app or terminal utility.
README is primarily Chinese and catalog quality of listed third-party items is not verified here.
Source discovery labeled it as Clients from awesome-selfhosted, which does not match the repo.

aiReview.summary: Community-curated Forgejo ecosystem list (clients, packaging, Actions, APIs). Useful as a resource, not a CLI or product itself.
evidence: README describes a curated list of Forgejo-related projects with sections including Clients, Tools, CI/CD, and API libraries.
Listed from awesome-selfhosted under Clients; Codeberg feed shows recent PRs (e.g. 207–210).
License section uses CC0; maintainers and contribution guidelines are documented.
uncertainty: Exact star/fork counts and contributor activity volume were not verified beyond README and atom feed.
Quality of every linked third-party client or package was not audited.
aiReview.tagline: Curated Forgejo clients, packaging, CI, and tools
aiReview.description: Browse official docs, public instances, CLIs, mobile apps, Actions, and API libraries for the Forgejo git forge.
pros: Maintained Codeberg list with official Forgejo resources, clients, packaging, and Actions coverage.
Marks inactive projects and points to licenses, docs, and public instances.
Recent pull activity and CC0 licensing for the list itself.
cons: It is a directory of other projects, not a command-line app or SDK.
Candidate title 'Clients' is only a subsection of a much broader list.

aiReview.summary: Self-hosted Node/TypeScript backend for GLANCE apps (sync, intents, media). Not a CLI; listing title “Clients” is a scrape artifact, and the server is still early (Phase 0, clients poll).
evidence: GitHub description: optional self-hosted backend for GLANCE apps with ZK sync, intents, media.
README Phase 0: SQLite, Express, better-sqlite3, Docker, healthz, shared Bearer token.
Source discovery used anchor text “Clients” on awesome-selfhosted, not the repo name.
uncertainty: Cannot independently verify cryptographic claims beyond “opaque envelopes, no server crypto.”
Activity recency and production use outside GLANCE clients are not verified.
aiReview.tagline: Self-hosted zero-knowledge sync backend for companion apps
aiReview.description: Run a Dockerized SQLite server that stores opaque sync envelopes, device intents, and media blobs with token auth.
pros: MIT-licensed Node/TypeScript server with Dockerfile, compose, tests, and GHCR images.
README documents schema, env/config, rate limits, CORS, and opaque envelope storage.
Listed from awesome-selfhosted, with 98 commits and CI/workflow files present.
cons: Not a command-line or terminal utility; it is a companion backend for GLANCE apps.
Low adoption (about 6 stars, 0 forks) and README marks client push as unfinished.
Auth defaults to a shared device token; Postgres is not implemented yet.

aiReview.summary: Maintained MIT-licensed self-hosted URL shortener in Rust with Docker images, a web UI, and a JSON-RPC-style API. It is a server/web app, not a CLI, so it is a weaker fit for a terminal-tools list despite being a solid GitHub-backed project.
evidence: GitHub description: simple self-hosted URL shortener written in Rust.
README features: Docker (~4.5–8.5 MB compressed images), SQLite, Actix Web backend, vanilla JS frontend.
Discovered from awesome-selfhosted/awesome-selfhosted README (Clients section).
MIT license, contributing guide, and security policy present on the repo.
uncertainty: Exact latest release date and current CVE status were not independently audited.
Source list titled the link as Clients, which may be a scrape/section mismatch.
Production security of password hashing and API key handling was not reviewed in code.
aiReview.tagline: Minimal self-hosted Rust URL shortener with Docker
aiReview.description: Self-host a small URL shortener with expiry, hit counts, optional public mode, SQLite, and Docker images under 10 MB RAM.
pros: Active GitHub repo with ~986 stars, 97 forks, 1089 commits, CI, Docker/GHCR images, and MIT license.
README documents Docker deploy, SQLite storage, API key/password auth, hit counting, expiry, QR codes, and a mobile-friendly UI.
Listed in awesome-selfhosted and ships docs for installation plus a security policy.
Author states the project is considered complete and will still receive bug and security fixes.
cons: It is a self-hosted web service, not a command-line or terminal utility.
README notes password auth is not encrypted in transit and recommends a reverse proxy for TLS.
Public-mode instances can allow unauthenticated link creation, which needs careful deployment.

aiReview.summary: Self-hosted, C-based URL shortener listed in awesome-selfhosted; tiny Forgejo project with almost no public traction, so treat as a niche homelab option pending a closer look at docs and maintenance.
evidence: Search snippet: “Dead-simple, super-minimal URL shortener written in C” with tags link-shortener.
Discovered repeatedly from awesome-selfhosted/awesome-selfhosted README.
Forge stats in snippet: Watch 1, Star 0, Fork 0.
uncertainty: Cannot verify README completeness, license, security model, or recent commit cadence from the fetched feed.
Cannot confirm whether the demo at short.swurl.xyz is still operated.
aiReview.tagline: Minimal self-hosted URL shortener written in C
aiReview.description: Self-host a tiny C URL shortener for simple link redirects without a large runtime stack.
pros: Described as a dead-simple, super-minimal URL shortener written in C.
Appears on awesome-selfhosted, so it is already in a curated self-host list.
Source is available on a public git forge with a documented demo host.
cons: Repository shows 0 stars and 0 forks, so community validation is effectively absent.
Hosted on a personal Forgejo instance rather than a widely mirrored GitHub project.
Public page content is thin; license, docs quality, and activity are hard to confirm from listing text alone.

aiReview.summary: Official Shlink apps listing of dashboard, web client, PowerShell module, and WordPress plugin—not a CLI itself. Weak fit if the directory targets command-line tools rather than URL-shortener GUIs.
evidence: Page states it is a curated list of official or third-party apps for Shlink.
Meta description: self-hosted PHP URL shortener with CLI and REST interfaces (the core product, not this URL).
Discovered as Clients in awesome-selfhosted README, not as a dedicated CLI repo.
uncertainty: Maintenance status and license of each listed third-party app were not verified beyond the listing.
Whether the directory intends the Shlink core CLI versus this apps page is unclear.
aiReview.tagline: Official list of URL-shortener clients and integrations
aiReview.description: Browse official and third-party apps that talk to a self-hosted URL shortener: dashboard, PWA, PowerShell, WordPress.
pros: Official project page listing first-party and third-party Shlink integrations.
Links to GitHub for Shlink Dashboard, web client, PSShlink, and Smol Links.
Describes a hosted web client at app.shlink.io plus self-host options.
cons: The URL is an apps catalog, not a single CLI or terminal utility.
Most listed products are GUIs or plugins; only PSShlink is command-line.
Page title in the source list is a generic “Clients” anchor, not a distinct tool.

aiReview.summary: BunkerWeb plugin documentation, not a CLI or terminal utility; the awesome-selfhosted “Clients” link is a mismatch for this directory.
evidence: URL https://docs.bunkerweb.io/latest/plugins documents BunkerWeb plugins, not clients.
Discovered from awesome-selfhosted README with anchor text “Clients”.
Rubric prefers GitHub-backed CLIs; this is WAF plugin documentation.
uncertainty: Whether awesome-selfhosted intended a different BunkerWeb URL.
Commercial vs community licensing beyond “open source WAF” in page meta.
aiReview.tagline: Docs for extending an open-source WAF with plugins
aiReview.description: Explains official BunkerWeb plugins, install paths, and how to add custom plugin features.
pros: Official MkDocs page lists maintained plugins with versions and GitHub paths.
Covers automatic zip install and manual install for Docker, Kubernetes, and Linux.
Includes plugin structure notes and links to bunkerweb-plugins and core plugin source.
cons: Candidate title “Clients” does not match this plugins documentation URL.
It is a product docs page, not a command-line app or standalone tool listing.
Swarm install path is marked deprecated on the same page.

aiReview.summary: Browser-based single-file wiki (TiddlyWiki-style, ~56KB HTML) listed under awesome-selfhosted Clients; not a command-line utility, so it fits a self-hosted/apps directory better than a CLI-focused list.
evidence: https://feather.wiki meta-description: A tiny tool for simple, self-contained wikis!; meta-version 1.9.1
Nav includes Downloads, Features, Known Limitations, Extensions, Extension Development, Publishing
codeberg.org/Alamantus/FeatherWiki and github.com/Alamantus/FeatherWiki described as a tiny self-contained JS wiki
Discovered from awesome-selfhosted README Clients section pointing at https://feather.wiki
uncertainty: Exact license text and current GitHub star counts were not verified from the repo README in this pass
Maintenance cadence and security of the HTML-file save model were not audited
awesome-selfhosted listing quality of the Clients row itself was not re-read
aiReview.tagline: Single-file, self-contained wiki that runs in the browser
aiReview.description: Create simple wikis and notebooks in one HTML file with extensions, publishing, and no server required.
pros: Official site documents a versioned 1.9.x product with downloads, learn pages, and extension APIs.
Primary development is on Codeberg (Alamantus/FeatherWiki) with a GitHub mirror.
Appears repeatedly in awesome-selfhosted as a self-contained wiki client.
cons: It is not a CLI or terminal workflow tool, which mismatches a command-line scoring rubric.
Page body content is not fully extractable from the site HTML in this review, so feature claims stay at meta/nav level.
Candidate title in the source list is the generic heading Clients rather than the product name.

aiReview.summary: Official SPDX page for Eclipse Public License 1.0, not a CLI or terminal utility. It is a legal license text scraped from a self-hosted list and does not belong in a command-line tools directory.
evidence: canonicalUrl is https://spdx.org/licenses/EPL-1.0.html
Fetched content is license metadata and EPL-1.0 agreement text, not software
sourceEvidence anchors are only the phrase Eclipse Public License, Version 1.0 in awesome-selfhosted README.md
Rubric targets CLIs and terminal utilities; this candidate fails that fit
uncertainty: Whether the target directory is strictly CLI-only versus mixed resources
Whether EPL-1.0 is still commonly chosen versus EPL-2.0
aiReview.tagline: OSI-approved copyleft license text on SPDX
aiReview.description: Publish the Eclipse Public License 1.0 identifier, OSI/FSF status, and full license terms for software relicensing.
pros: Hosted on SPDX with license ID EPL-1.0 and OSI/FSF flags.
Includes the full EPL 1.0 text and official cross-references.
Page is maintained as part of the SPDX license list, not a gist or blog roundup.
cons: It is a legal document, not a command-line app or developer tool.
Discovery came from license-name links in awesome-selfhosted, not a tools catalog.
EPL 1.0 is superseded in practice by later EPL versions for new projects.

aiReview.summary: This is the SPDX text of the Eclipse Public License 2.0, not a CLI, SDK, or app. It was scraped from awesome-selfhosted license links and does not belong in a tools directory.
evidence: canonicalUrl is https://spdx.org/licenses/EPL-2.0.html
Page is SPDX license metadata plus EPL-2.0 legal text
sourceEvidence repeated from awesome-selfhosted README license anchors only
uncertainty: Whether the directory ever intends to index licenses as first-class entries
aiReview.tagline: OSI-approved copyleft license with secondary-license option
aiReview.description: Official SPDX listing of EPL-2.0, including OSI/FSF status, cross-references, and full license text.
pros: Canonical SPDX identifier EPL-2.0 with OSI-approved and FSF Libre flags.
Includes full license text and links to eclipse.org and opensource.org.
Documents secondary-license (GPL) handling via Exhibit A.
cons: Not a software product, CLI, or self-hosted app.
Discovery source is a license hyperlink in awesome-selfhosted, not a listed tool.
No installable interface, API, or workflow utility to catalog.

aiReview.summary: Official Proton TypeScript monorepo for Mail, Calendar, Drive, Account, VPN, Pass, and related web apps; GPL-3.0 source, not a CLI or self-hosted mail stack.
evidence: GitHub README describes a pnpm monorepo hosting Proton Mail, Calendar, Drive, Account, VPN, Pass, Wallet, Lumo, and Meet.
Repo metadata: ~5.6k stars, TypeScript, GNU GPL v3.0.
Discovered from AwesomeHomelab as “ProtonMail Web Client”, which mismatches a CLI-focused rubric.
uncertainty: Cannot verify self-hostability of full Proton backend from this repo alone.
Issue/PR activity and security posture beyond public GitHub metadata were not fully audited.
aiReview.tagline: Open-source monorepo of Proton encrypted web apps
aiReview.description: Build and run Proton Mail, Calendar, Drive, Account, VPN, Pass, and related web clients from a pnpm TypeScript monorepo.
pros: Official ProtonMail/WebClients repo with GPL-3.0 license and active TypeScript monorepo structure.
Documents pnpm workspaces, install, and start commands for multiple Proton web applications.
Thousands of stars and a large applications/packages tree indicate a maintained production codebase.
cons: This is browser web-client source, not a command-line utility or self-hosted server.
Running clients still depends on Proton’s backend services rather than a standalone homelab mail stack.

aiReview.summary: Svelte 4 web app that mimics a terminal in the browser, with themes, todos, calc, weather, and Docker deploy. It is a portfolio-style site, not a native CLI or system terminal.
evidence: README: terminal-style website, Svelte 4, Vite, Tailwind, Docker ghcr.io/m4tt72/terminal.
GitHub metadata: 1564 stars, 290 forks, MIT, TypeScript, 6 open issues.
Listed from AwesomeHomelab as M4TT72 Terminal, not as a CLI package.
uncertainty: Recent commit cadence and security of curl-like URL fetching were not inspected in source.
Live site term.fathi.me was not verified.
aiReview.tagline: Browser terminal UI with themes and toy commands
aiReview.description: Run a Svelte terminal-style website with themes, history, tab complete, weather, and Docker. Not a native shell.
pros: MIT-licensed TypeScript/Svelte 4 project with Vitest, Playwright, and claimed 85%+ coverage.
Ships Docker image, compose file, CI workflows, and documented theme/command set.
About 1.5k GitHub stars and an active v3 (Svelte) README versus an unmaintained React v2 branch.
cons: It is a website demo, not a command-line or system terminal utility.
Commands include HTTP fetch and third-party weather (wttr.in), which are browser-side conveniences rather than production tooling.

aiReview.summary: Official Google terminal TUI for prompting and monitoring Antigravity agents (natural language, subagents, slash commands). Fits a CLI/productivity directory; verify install/docs still match the product page.
evidence: https://antigravity.google/product/antigravity-cli describes Work in Natural Language, Subagents, Slash Commands, and TUI first-launch setup.
Install CTA points to /download#antigravity-cli; docs to /docs/cli/getting-started.
Site mentions Gemini 4 Argon for Google AI Pro and Ultra, implying Google account/subscription coupling.
uncertainty: Exact pricing tier for CLI-only use was not verified on /pricing.
Open-source status, update cadence, and OS support were not confirmed from a repository.
aiReview.tagline: Terminal TUI to run and monitor coding agents
aiReview.description: Stay in the terminal to prompt agents, run parallel subagents, and configure MCP, skills, and keybindings via slash commands.
pros: Official Google product page describes a terminal-first TUI for agent sessions.
Documents parallel subagents, slash commands for plugins/MCP/skills/hooks, and /config and /keybindings.
Install and getting-started docs are linked from the product site.
cons: Requires the Google Antigravity ecosystem rather than a standalone open-source CLI.
Pricing, license, and GitHub source are not stated on the product page itself.

aiReview.summary: Official Google Antigravity product blog (Aug 24, 2026) describing in-app Git VCS controls and an embedded terminal—not a standalone CLI. Useful as product documentation, not as a command-line utility to list.
evidence: canonical URL https://antigravity.google/blog/vcs-and-terminal/
Title and byline: Improving the version control experience, The Antigravity Team, Aug 24, 2026
Content describes Git VCS Controls in the right-side panel and an embedded terminal tab
Mentions views: Agent Edits, Uncommitted, Branch; stage/commit; git status / go test in terminal
Rubric prefers maintained GitHub-backed CLIs over product blogs
uncertainty: Actual product availability, pricing tiers, and UI fidelity vs the interactive preview
Whether the parent directory is meant to list product blogs vs CLIs
aiReview.tagline: In-app Git review, diffs, commits, and embedded terminal
aiReview.description: Describes Git VCS controls and an embedded terminal in Antigravity 2.0 so you can review diffs, stage, commit, and run commands without leaving the app.
pros: Official Google Antigravity blog post with a dated product announcement and clear feature description.
Explains Git-grounded diffs (agent edits, uncommitted, branch vs origin/main), stage/commit UI, and an embedded terminal.
Includes an interactive simulation of the side panel workflows.
Page is live on antigravity.google with standard article metadata.
cons: It is a product blog, not a GitHub-backed CLI or installable terminal utility.
Features apply only inside Antigravity 2.0, not as a standalone tool.
Does not document a public CLI API or open-source repository for the VCS panel itself.

aiReview.summary: Official docs for a keyboard-first terminal client that runs agentic coding workflows in local shells, remote environments, and SSH, with a linked getting-started path and CLI reference.
evidence: Page copy: keyboard-first terminal client for local shells, remote cloud environments, and SSH.
CLI labeled agy · v1.2+ with links to /docs/getting-started?tab=cli and /docs/cli/reference/.
Canonical URL is official docs on antigravity.google; candidate discovered from curated docs home.
uncertainty: Cannot verify open-source status, install method, or exact pricing from this overview.
Runtime quality, maintenance cadence, and GitHub presence were not independently verified beyond the docs site.
aiReview.tagline: Keyboard-first terminal client for agentic coding workflows
aiReview.description: Run agent workflows in local shells, remote clouds, and SSH with a keyboard-first terminal client and documented CLI reference.
pros: Official documentation describes a terminal client (version 1.2+) for local, remote, and SSH sessions.
Docs link to a CLI getting-started guide and a CLI reference manual.
The surface is presented as a first-class product alongside desktop, IDE, and SDK interfaces.
cons: The overview page is a multi-surface product chooser, not a standalone CLI README or GitHub repo.
Pricing, license, and install packaging are not stated on this page.

aiReview.summary: Official Google Antigravity docs for installing and authenticating the agy CLI (and related surfaces). Useful as a reference, but it is documentation rather than a standalone CLI project.
evidence: Canonical docs at antigravity.google describe Antigravity CLI (agy) authentication and install flags.
Personal Google plans (Free, Pro, Ultra), Gemini API keys, and Gemini Enterprise/ADC are documented.
Candidate was discovered as a curated docs link titled Installation and auth, not a CLI source repo.
uncertainty: Cannot verify CLI maintenance, license, or GitHub presence from this page alone.
Cannot confirm current product availability or pricing beyond plan names mentioned in docs.
aiReview.tagline: Official install and auth docs for the agy CLI
aiReview.description: Documents Google account, Gemini API key, SSH OAuth, and ADC authentication for the agy CLI and related surfaces.
pros: Official Google documentation covering CLI keyring, SSH OAuth, Gemini API key, and ADC auth.
Includes concrete config paths, env vars, and troubleshooting for API-key mode.
Describes installation script flags such as --skip-aliases and --skip-path.
cons: The URL is an install/auth guide, not a GitHub-backed CLI repository or tool homepage.
The page also covers App, IDE, and SDK auth, so it is not CLI-only.
Pricing and binary distribution details live on other pages, not this one.

aiReview.summary: Official Google Antigravity getting-started docs (CLI tab) covering install of the agy TUI, first session, artifact review, and related surfaces. Useful as maintained vendor CLI documentation rather than a standalone open-source tool.
evidence: Page redirects from /docs/cli/tutorial to /docs/getting-started?tab=cli.
Install uses curl install.sh | bash and PowerShell irm | iex; binary named agy.
CLI section includes workspace trust, color scheme, rendering mode, Ctrl+R review, Y to approve.
Candidate discovered from antigravity.google/docs/home curated listing as official-web.
uncertainty: Cannot verify CLI source, license, or GitHub maintenance from this docs page.
Cannot confirm pricing, quotas, or regional availability.
Some IDE version numbers (e.g. Xcode 27, VS 2026) look unusually future-dated and were not independently verified.
aiReview.tagline: Official CLI install and first-session agent tutorial
aiReview.description: Install the agy CLI, launch a terminal agent session, review artifacts, and run tasks in a local workspace.
pros: Official Google documentation with concrete agy install commands for macOS, Linux, and Windows.
Walks through first TUI session, artifact review keys, and a sample agent task.
Links related install, authentication, and enterprise guides.
Documents default binary paths and version check via agy --version.
cons: The listed URL redirects to a multi-surface getting-started page, not a CLI-only tutorial.
Source listing title is only “Tutorial” with no independent GitHub CLI repo.
Requires Google/Gemini authentication; product pricing is not stated on the page.

aiReview.summary: Official Google docs for Antigravity CLI settings, slash commands, and keybindings. Useful as a reference page for the TUI CLI, not a standalone tool listing.
evidence: Page title and body: CLI settings and tips, JSON config path, /config overlay, slash commands, keybindings.json.
canonicalUrl is official docs; discoveredFrom curated_readme with repeated Using Antigravity CLI anchors.
Mentions --dangerously-skip-permissions as a documented override, which is a safety-relevant flag.
uncertainty: CLI source, license, pricing, and maintenance status are not on this page.
Relationship between Gemini and Antigravity branding is not fully specified here.
aiReview.tagline: Official CLI settings, shortcuts, and keybinding reference
aiReview.description: Configure JSON settings, slash commands, permissions, and custom keybindings for the Gemini Antigravity terminal CLI.
pros: Official documentation hosted on antigravity.google covering CLI settings, tips, and keybindings.
Documents configuration at ~/.gemini/antigravity-cli/settings.json and flag overrides such as --sandbox.
Includes a command/shortcut table plus default keybindings and how to edit or reset keybindings.json.
cons: This URL is a usage/settings page, not a GitHub-backed CLI repository or installable binary.
Does not document installation, full command surface, or licensing on this page.

aiReview.summary: Official Antigravity CLI documentation covering plugins, terminal sandboxing, slash commands, settings.json, and subagents. Suitable as a docs entry for a Google agent CLI, not as a standalone tool listing.
evidence: Fetched https://antigravity.google/docs/cli/features: plugins under ~/.gemini/antigravity-cli/, agy plugin, enableTerminalSandbox, slash command table, /agents subagents.
Candidate type is web_url from curated official docs; riskFlags empty.
Rubric prefers maintained CLI tooling; this URL is official CLI feature docs rather than the tool itself.
uncertainty: Could not verify CLI license, GitHub presence, or current maintenance from this page alone.
Overall product pricing beyond one paid teamwork feature is not fully specified.
aiReview.tagline: Official docs for an agent CLI, plugins, and sandbox
aiReview.description: Documents plugin install, OS-level terminal sandbox, slash commands, settings, and parallel subagents for a Google agent CLI.
pros: Official Google documentation with concrete commands, paths, and JSON config examples.
Covers plugin marketplace/local/GitHub install, nsjail/sandbox-exec/AppContainer isolation, and slash-command reference.
Describes subagent panel, approvals, and permissions allow/deny lists.
cons: Page is a features doc, not a GitHub-backed CLI repository or installable binary.
Title in the candidate is only “Features,” which is weak for a directory listing.
Some capabilities (for example teamwork-preview) are noted as paid-plan only.

aiReview.summary: Official Antigravity CLI docs covering verification loops, explore-plan-execute prompting, workspace rules, permission modes, TUI session controls, and non-interactive scripting. Suitable as a companion resource for that CLI, not a standalone tool.
evidence: Page title and content: CLI best practices on antigravity.google.
Mentions GEMINI.md/AGENTS.md, ~/.gemini/antigravity-cli/settings.json, and agy -p.
Discovered repeatedly from official docs home curated links.
uncertainty: Cannot verify CLI maturity, GitHub presence, or whether Antigravity is generally available.
Pricing of the underlying product is not stated on this page.
aiReview.tagline: Official CLI workflows, rules, and session controls
aiReview.description: Learn verification loops, planning prompts, GEMINI.md rules, sandbox permissions, rewind/fork, and one-shot -p scripting for the CLI.
pros: Official documentation with concrete prompt examples and settings.json fields.
Covers tests-first verification, explore-plan-execute, and workspace rule files.
Documents TUI controls (esc, /rewind, /fork) and non-interactive agy -p usage.
cons: Tied to Antigravity/Gemini CLI rather than a general-purpose CLI utility.
Does not ship an installable tool; it is a documentation page only.
